A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MediConfusion, with the same core benchmark and curation pipeline. All 17 pages of v1 and 24 pages of v2, including their appendices, support comparison; retained figures, tables, and prompts can be matched.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of nine models on MediConfusion, including overall and category-specific results in Tables 1–2 and qualitative failure analyses.

after.justification: V2 retains those results, evaluates thirteen models, and adds original experiments on prompting, fine-tuning, dataset difficulty, visual representations, and response aggregation in Appendices C–H.

M1.justification: The original benchmark curation procedure is retained, but Appendix H introduces substantive model and inference adaptations: concatenating DINOv2 and CLIP features in LLaVA-Med with alignment/instruction training, and GPT-4o response selection through oracle scoring, self-ranking, and majority voting. These are actual procedural additions beyond expanded documentation.

E1.justification: The original 352-question benchmark and nine medical categories remain unchanged. Appendix E adds an easier ROCO-derived VQA scenario with dissimilar pairs and less demanding questions, such as anatomical-region identification, alongside an unfiltered hard-pair control. This extends test coverage within the existing radiology domain.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 expand the evaluated model set from nine to thirteen by adding DeepSeek-VL2, Molmo-7B, o1, and Gemini 2.0 Flash. All original models remain, substantially broadening the open-source and proprietary comparisons.

E3.justification: The original evaluation settings are retained, while new experiments introduce materially different protocols: an 84-pair training/92-pair test split with up to 1,000 fine-tuning epochs, matched 988-pair easy and unfiltered controls, and alternative response-selection budgets. Appendix H.2 also lowers the free-form score-gap threshold from 3 to 2 specifically for the new oracle experiment.

E4.justification: V2 retains v1's category breakdowns, failure patterns, and visual-prompt discussion, then adds extensive analyses in Appendices C–H. These test prompt sensitivity, fine-tuning, pair difficulty and radiologist filtering, similarity across encoders, reversed pair-selection criteria, feature fusion, and response aggregation—several previously untested explanations and possible remedies for failure.

E5.justification: Appendix C/Table 4 newly reports means and standard deviations across ten random samples for each of eleven prompts for GPT-4o, InstructBLIP, and LLaVA-Med. V1 provides point estimates without comparable uncertainty reporting. This addition is confined to the prompting study; it does not establish repeated evaluation of the original main results.

E6.justification: Original model scores in Tables 1–2 are retained, but new models and appendix experiments add substantial results. Gemini 2.0 Flash reaches 29.55% set accuracy versus the 25% random baseline, changing the below-chance finding. GPT-4o achieves 98.38% set accuracy on the new easy variant. V2 also introduces a discrepancy: Table 6 gives LLaVA-Med's original-benchmark PS set accuracy as 0.00%, whereas Table 1 reports 1.14% in both versions.

T1.justification: The original scoring definitions and argument about the limits of language-only priors are retained. Neither version presents theorems or proofs. V2's contrastive-learning explanation and experimental threshold variations do not introduce formal theoretical results.

C1.justification: The introduction and conclusion narrow the below-random-performance claim from all existing models to most models, reflecting the expanded evaluation. The benchmark and failure-analysis contributions remain unchanged. The abstract still retains the broader 'all available models' statement, making the qualification inconsistent across v2.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations involving contrastive-pretraining shortcuts, prompt-format sensitivity, limitations of fine-tuning with a frozen vision encoder, and the combined demands of visual discrimination and medical knowledge. It also acknowledges that auxiliary datasets lack radiologist verification and interprets feature-fusion and sampling experiments as insufficient remedies. These substantially expand v1's failure-pattern and OCR/Gemini discussion.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's existing prompt templates and model settings, v2 documents additional model versions and decoding parameters, eleven MC prompts, split construction, the fine-tuning learning-rate search and selected 5×10^-6 rate, training duration, and token averaging for encoder comparisons. The advertised repository also changes from MShahabSepehri/MediConfusion to AIF4S/MediConfusion.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for the new models, Micro-Bench, contrastive-learning shortcomings, best-of-N selection, and self-consistency. These support localized extensions; the positioning as a medical failure benchmark extending confusing-image-pair research remains substantially unchanged. Citation-style changes do not constitute new research positioning.

P1.justification: The six-section main narrative and most existing prose are retained. V2 makes localized wording and explanatory edits, converts numbered related-work subsections into topic paragraphs, changes citation style, and revises author/publication information. Appendices C–H organize the added scientific material without extensively rewriting the retained text.

P2.justification: V2 adds Figures 6–9 showing fine-tuning curves, an easy question pair, encoder-similarity histograms, and reversed-selection examples, plus Tables 4–10 for the new studies and prompts. Tables 1–3 gain model rows. Existing Figures 1–5 retain their image content but are repositioned or resized, and table captions and appendix layouts are reformatted.

improvement.justification: V1 mainly establishes low benchmark scores; v2 substantially strengthens validation by testing prompt sensitivity, adding easy/unfiltered controls, examining multiple encoders, and investigating adaptation and response aggregation. These directly address previously untested explanations for the observed failures and add useful reproducibility information. The unchanged universal claim in the abstract and the inconsistent LLaVA-Med entry in Table 6 weaken reporting consistency, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support.
